full_judgment:
The presumption would, therefore, appear on principle to be that, in the case of a F.O.B. contract, the seller intends to fulfil his contract and that the property is intended to puss and does pass on shipment". 

 It is stated in the same book at page 727 that "it is now clear that the fact that an F.O.B. contract provides only for handing over of bills of lading against payment does not affect seller's obligation under the contract to pass the property to the buyer on shipment and it is difficult to justify, in the case of F.O.B. contracts, the presumption ...............that property is to pass only on payment" 

 (4) The mere fact that a F.O.B. contract provides for banding over of bills of lading against payment does not justify a presumption that property is to pass on payment; 

 Thus, even if the seller has retained the shipping documents for securing the price of goods by providing that the documents shall be delivered on payment, there is a presumption in a F.O.B. contract that property passes on shipment unless a contrary intention has been expressed. In the instant case the defence is a total denial of the contract. The defendant has no case that the intention of the parties was that the property in the goods would pass on payment against delivery of shipping documents or at any other time. In the absence of any such case of the defendant either in the written statement or at evidence, we are of the opinion that there is no scope for the learned Advocate for the appellant to argue that the parties in-tended that the property should not pass on shipment but at a subsequent time with the observation above we now come to the consideration' of the decision reported in 26 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 329 relied on by the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant. It appears that in that case the plaintiff's case was that delivery took place as soon as the goods were put on board the ship at Karachi and upon shipment, the property in the goods, passed to the plaintiff. On the other hand, the defence case was that the property in the goods was intended to pass on the date the defendant was notified to retire the shipping documents. In that case the parties came up with two specific cases and the defendant came out with a case which was an exception to the normal incidence of passing of property in a F.O.B. contract. But such is not the case here the facts of the present case are distinguishable from the facts of the reported case. In the present case, in the absence of any intention expressed to the contrary, it must be held that property in the goods passed on shipment notwithstanding the stipulation that the shipping documents shall be sent to the plaintiff's Chittagong Office and will be retired by the defendant from that office on payment It may also be observed that the invoices were prepared in the name of the defendant and in the invoices the defendant was charged for freight and insurance premium paid on his account, the defendant was name as the consignee in the bills of landing, the defendant was repeatedly requested to retire the shipping documents, and the goods were sold after clearing on giving lawyer's notice to the Defendant, and the sale price was credited to defdt's account (Ext. 9(b) These also support plaintiff's case and furnish evidence that in default of defendants retirement of the documents on payment plaintiff sold the goods which he could do in exercise of his seller's lien The plaintiff's conduct is in no way inconsistent with, or positively put, is quite in conformity with the normal incidence of a F.O.B, contract that property passes on shipment and with commercial practice.
